en: When they came to a turn,
Toruchaar, the swift steed,
His eyes flashed like a stag's,
Of the moon-yellow plain,
The renowned, watchful Joloy
Entered its throat.
Hard upon his very tracks,
Destroying his peace,
Manas pursued him until he turned pale.
Not a mountain the size of an ankle bone,
Not a hollow to crouch and hide in,
The Kytay called it Dyngsha,
It was a desert of forty days' travel.
Not a drop of water anywhere,
Not a pinch of grass to eat,
Following the edge of that desert,
Joloy went onward.
Unable to find his bearings,
Despairing of his borrowed life,
Joloy went fleeing,
“If the blood-shedder catches me, he will devour me,” he said,
Great Joloy, sunk in despair,
Lost all hope of his precious life.
His brows contracted a handspan,
He rumbled in furious anger.
What could poor Joloy do?
He scolded Achbuudan:
“You were a winged tulpar steed;
A curse has struck you,” he said.
“If the bloodstained one catches me, he will show no mercy;
Death has overtaken me,” he said.
The unbelievers' Joloy
Was a thoroughly formidable rogue.
A great sorcerer, an enchanter,
That wretch could conjure weather.
The earth split as it flashed along;
That confounded Toruchaar
Toward Joloy's Achbuudan,
Drew close, about to catch him.
At Joloy riding ahead,
Manas thundered his challenge:
“You damned slave Joloy,
Keep running—let me see!
Let me spill your blood like water.
Turn back if you are a man;
Let us grapple and see!
Dog with your skirt slit a handspan,
Mindless, rotten dog!
If you keep fleeing like this,
Unless I drive you into a pit,
Unless I heap suffering upon you,
Unless I pursue you to Beejin,
Unless I loose my fierce wrath,
Unless I cut off your head with my sword,
May I die instead of living!
Black Kalmyk, do not flee;
Let us grapple and see.
If you keep fleeing like this,
Your flight will not make me leave you.
You have fallen into my wrath;
Like a curse I will ensnare you.
If I catch you now, I will show no mercy.
'I died without being able to wrestle,'
You will say, left with regret.
You will see terrible wrath;
You will die fleeing like a woman!
If I catch you, Kalmyk,
I will give you a terrible surprise,
You hulking unbeliever!
If I catch you,
I will cut off your head with my sword!
I am destruction born for the Kytay;
I will make you pay dearly.
You killed many of my forefathers;
I will take revenge for that!
Great Altay, with its streams and springs—
I have no livestock left to drive up there.
You yourself attacked and started the quarrel.
Death-seeking Kytay, just wait;
I have no life to spare from death.
My wrath has risen; I stand firm.
You have sorely roused my anger.
I will launch a campaign and fight;
Now I will surely attack one of you.
You would not leave a peaceful man in peace;
Have you roused my anger?
I will attack your Kakanchy;
Bakburchun is my adversary.
I will gird my waist tight.
You have fled, my black Kalmyk;
I will pursue you all the way to Beejin!
If I chance to catch you,
The hollow of your ribs
I will tear apart with a crunch.
I will spill every drop of your blood.
You damned Kalmyk,
Now you are caught in suffering.
Leading seven thousand champions,
Why did you attack my land?
To attack my land,
To bind and capture me—
The Kytay who migrated from Beejin
Have not five cities' hosts of migrants.
Ill-willed Kalmyk, just wait;
Your seven forefathers have no blood debt to avenge!”
Manas came on in fury,
Addressing lion Joloy.
When Manas shouted these words,
The fleeing Kalmyk Joloy
Lost his composure.
When he glanced behind him,
Generous Manas, the leopard,
Appeared ready to drink blood.
Toruchaar beneath him
Was visible when he could be seen;
When unseen, the confounded horse
Dissolved into blue smoke,
Galloping over every rise and hollow,
Heaving up mountains of dust.
Toruchaar beneath him
Flew flashing like a cloud.
The confounded beast had come
Close to Achbuudan.
When Manas drew near,
At the yellow marsh of Bylkyldak,
Full of forest mixed with willow scrub,
Unable to find a way out, he panicked.
The gallant hero Joloy
Fled into the forest.
Khan Joloy of the Kalmyks
Was himself a weather-conjuring wretch.
Having entered the forest,
The rain-making weather stone
He lifted and put in the water.
Cloud appeared down below;
Blue across the face of the earth,
A ground mist descended and covered it.
Whistling in from every side,
A cold wind struck.
Bulging over the mountaintop,
A black cloud stood.
The cloud flew and shifted;
Six-grooved hail poured from the sky,
With white-streaked rain and sleet—
May God never let you see it!
The mountain summits were covered;
Mist appeared in the hollows.
All the foothills were pelted with hail;
All the lower slopes were drenched in rain.
Every pit was clogged;
Every ditch was overwhelmed.
Pouring down from the heavens,
Six-grooved hail and sleet
Tore up the earth's surface.
A flood surged and swept along;
Of the trees in the ravines,
The roots stood stripped and exposed.
Boulders like resting camels and cattle
Lay stark on the plain.
Logs like resting camels
Jutted every which way.
The entire forest was engulfed.
Wherever you looked in the mountains,
Floodwater swept through, laying waste,
As he worked his strange weather magic.
That damned Joloy escaped;
Everything between was laid waste.
A summer day became cold winter.
On lord Manas's face
Cold ice formed four fingerbreadths thick.
From the direction of prayer,
A cold wind blew whistling.
The shrouding clouds scattered;
It grew brilliantly bright,
And Allah's sunshine broke through.
Dark steam billowed from the earth.
Grieving that he could not find Joloy,
Mighty Manas, the blood-drinking slayer,
Turned back toward Altay.
Following a solitary path,
Looking whenever it came into view,
He watched the distant Altay mountain.
Pale, mottled haze filled the sky.
Having had his many champions slaughtered,
That hellish Joloy escaped.
Ah, that proud, swaggering hero!
There he came on in a rage,
Chest thrust out like a hungry lion,
Darkening with anger,
With the eyes of a hunting eagle.
The noble lion growled;
The poor hero strode in fury,
Finding no mountain to strike against,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no road to travel,
Finding no army to attack.
As he skirted Altay's mountain,
As the noble gray-maned hero came,
Sixty tulpars, a host of swift steeds,
Were being driven before a rider.
Looming up directly in front of him,
The giant Kaman appeared.
When he saw the giant Kaman,
Even an early word seemed late;
Blood-drinking, bloodstained Manas,
Longing for a clash,
Watched with doubled eagerness:
“The giant Kaman with scissor ears—
Let me grapple with him!
The racers he has taken as booty,
Let me snatch them from his midst!
While my mighty head is still on me,
To have the racers driven off,
How could I yield them as booty?
With that slave who thinks himself strong,
Let me clash and see!
While my falcon head is still on me,
How could I give up my tulpars?
He is a giant who came from Beejin;
Let me face him and see!
Let me unleash fierce wrath;
With that mountain-sized giant,
Let me clash once!
If fate has come, let me die.
That mountain-sized champion—
Let me meet him in a furious charge
And try a fight to the finish!
Kaman the giant thinks himself a hero;
Let me charge and thrust my spear.
With that dog who thinks himself so skilled,
Let me grapple once.
'There is no remedy for fate,' I say;
Let me strike a crushing blow.
'Black Kalmyk, this is for you,' I say;
Let me avenge my far-off wrongs.”
The giant Kaman with scissor ears
Had mighty courage and terrible fury.
He was a fearsome giant among his kind.
Among spearmen, he had
Outstanding distinction.
Destroying whoever grappled with him,
He possessed great skill.
When he met an enemy in combat,
His voice could drive the soul out.
Things went as he wished;
Whoever fell squarely into his hands,
He mowed down like young reeds.
When his courage rose and he attacked,
All those who clashed with him
He simply sucked in, horse and all.
Many who grappled with him
He slaughtered outright.
Once the seven Beejins rose up,
On this side of Kap-Too,
On the far border of the Kytay,
At Kyyanger, at Kapsang-Too,
